newsitem.title: SPAIN: Size is everything as more Spanish builders merge.
newsitem.headline: Size is everything as more Spanish builders merge.

text.p: A few big, tough construction companies are emerging in Spain from a frenzied round of mergers, offering good value for shareholders because size is important in competing for private business, analysts said.

Wednesday's announcement of a merger between OCP Construcciones and Gines Navarro was just the most recent in a series of deals that has reshaped the sector, boosting efficiency, cutting jobs and improving the prospects for shareholders.
"Firms have to risk more money and need higher technological investment than in the past. Size has become an important factor," said Lucia Granda of Beta Capital in Madrid.
"The industry has been through a clear concentration process for several months already," said Paz Sainz, analyst at Benito y Monjardin in Madrid.
Gines Navarro and OCP shares powered ahead on the merger news, climbing above the 15 percent opening limit, and dealers expect further gains.

Today's deal follows a merger between Cubiertas and Entrecanales into Acciona group, and a deal between Spain's two biggest group's Dragados and Fomento de Construcciones Y Contratas to boost their activities. Some deals were driven by a lack of state business.
"That was due to fewer public investments. Now new firms have to be ready to attract a higher level of private financing. This is why size has become important now," she added.
According to the firm's association Seopan, during 1996 production in the sector fell one percent, with this year expected to remain dull and a full recovery seen only for 1999.
But the outlook is improving, analysts said.

"Now (the building sector) is facing a better future. It can attract more private financing, while the government could be prompted to use its privatisation receipts to make new investment," said Juan Cueto, chief analyst at Ibersecurities in Madrid.
But the improvement is especially due to the fact that firms are making themselves more competitive.
"The future is bright because through mergers firms are expected to also save money, and not only to improve their financial status," said Benito y Monjardin's Sainz.
The Spanish buiding sector is expected to reduce its workforce this year by 25,000 from a total of 1.175 million at the end of 1996, according to the firm's association.
"Gines and OCP can gain 20 percent more than actual levels, other shares in the sector maybe less," said Cueto.
Together, the two firms will have turnover of 350 billion pesetas, a bit more than the new Acciona.
"They (Gines and OCP) were both undervalued and the merger is adding to them new pressure," said Granda.
Dealers are also speculating over the fact that after the merger the current owners of Gines Navarro could be interested in reducing their stakes, increasing the free floating shares.
"This is also likely to boost the value of their shares," a Madrid-based dealer said.
Other analysts suggested the merger process had not yet come to an end.
"Acciona, which wanted to be the main Spanish building firm after Dragados and FCC, may be looking nervously at the Gines OCP merger and begin to look for something else," said Granda.
